reasons: The excerpt explicitly directs selecting one persona rather than addressing menopause and muscle growth together above the fold, and routing menopause and muscle-building audiences to separate relevant PDPs and landing pages.
The candidate preserves the above-the-fold limitation and does not invent a persona-selection method.
The excerpt expressly says a changed offer requires a different PDP and gives bundle, single-product, and different-product offers as examples requiring unique PDPs.
The excerpt says that, although angles can be stacked on one landing page, keeping the angle the same generally provides better conversion and continuity.
The candidate does not turn the source's general performance rationale into an unsupported numerical claim.
The action is directly supported: the excerpt recommends specificity over broad application on any landing page and in any ad.

Its trigger unnecessarily restricts the recommendation to supplements that can be presented through many angles. The source states the recommendation applies anytime on landing pages and ads, not only under that supplement-specific example.
The excerpt directly contrasts broad benefit-listing ads with the instruction to problem-agitate into one issue and speak to one specific person.
The candidate's single-problem formulation is supported by the surrounding specificity discussion.
The excerpt describes the stated mismatch: an arthritis-focused ad leading to a PDP that presents the product as a solution to many unrelated problems can produce distrust and worse conversion.
The candidate correctly presents this as a warning and does not supply an unsubstantiated magnitude of conversion loss.
The excerpt explicitly identifies product-focused rather than person-focused copy as a common landing-page mistake and says copy should be benefit-led rather than feature-led.
The core action is supported: the source says every landing-page copy line should answer the 'so what' question.
The trigger narrows the instruction to feature statements, even though the source says it applies anytime something is said.

The completion criterion makes reinforcement with a benefit mandatory for every line based on a single feature example. The broader source requirement is to explain why the statement matters; it does not specify that every line must be completed by a benefit statement.
The candidate accurately identifies this as an example given by the source, in which 'triple peptide complex' is connected to 'firmer skin in four weeks.'
The excerpt directly instructs writers to lead with the outcome and then justify it with the feature, using the same firmer-skin/triple-peptide ordering reflected in the candidate.
The source supports using pain-led or benefit-led headlines and says this is among the few landing-page elements worth split testing.

The trigger states categorically that the headline is above the fold and seen by everyone, whereas the source says this is only 'typically' the case. The candidate should retain that qualifier or avoid presenting it as a prerequisite.
The source explicitly calls repositioning oneself as 'one of one' step one of copywriting, in the context of a product that is not genuinely unique or otherwise sounds like competitors.
The source recommends exporting existing reviews and asking an LLM to identify feedback that differentiates the product.
Having reviews is expressed as 'Hopefully you have some reviews,' not as a firm prerequisite. The candidate should not convert that hope into a required condition.
The source only says the LLM will 'hopefully' produce something, so unique output is not a supported completion criterion.

The stated depends_on relation to already repositioning the product as 'one of one' is not established. Review analysis is presented as a tactic for finding differentiation and supporting that repositioning, not as an action requiring repositioning to have already been completed.

The source supports tactically combining complementary benefits as a possible way to create unique positioning and explicitly warns against merely stringing together generic benefits or treating shipping, service, and delivery as differentiators.

The depends_on relation to the separate 'reposition as one of one' action is not supported as a prerequisite. Combining benefits is offered as one of the tactics for accomplishing differentiated positioning, rather than something that must wait until repositioning is already complete.
The source does offer Bloom's women-focused greens-powder positioning as an example of white-space repositioning.

However, the speaker explicitly qualifies the example with 'I might be getting this wrong' and says Bloom's formula 'might have been better. I'm not sure.' The claim recounts the positioning account categorically; the caveat should be incorporated into the claim rather than left only as an unknown.

omissions.description: The source recommends pursuing white-space (or 'purple ocean') repositioning as the strongest differentiation approach, beyond the more general instruction to position the product as unique.
omissions.quote: Now, the best thing you can possibly do here is reposition yourself into whites space. Or you could think about this as a purple ocean.

source_limitations: The excerpt begins mid-thought ('views.') and ends during an example, so adjacent context that could define prior categories or complete the Bloom discussion is absent.
The material is a spoken-style transcript with apparent transcription errors and informal terminology, which can make exact tool names and wording uncertain.
Several performance and consumer-behavior statements are asserted by the speaker without evidence, measurements, test designs, or applicable conditions in the excerpt.
The Bloom example is expressly hedged by the speaker as potentially inaccurate, and the speaker is unsure whether the formula itself differed.
